ARTICLE IN PRESS Prioritizing Global Equity in Migration Research Abstract Research shows that global knowledge production is unequal, leading to disparities in understanding across topics, geographies, and populations. This inequality is particularly concerning for critical social and political issues like immigration, one of the most divisive topics worldwide. Using Scopus bibliometric data from 1996 to 2022, we compile a comprehensive corpus of over 125,000 migration-related publications spanning all academic disciplines and interdisciplinary fields. By analyzing their content, we identify gaps, measure missed opportunities, and examine the demographic over- and under-representation of countries. Our findings reveal that some countries and subregions remain systematically underrepresented despite S having significant migrant populations. Key factors influencing this underrepresentation include research S investment and geographic location, with African countries, Central Asia, and Latin America and the E Caribbean being particularly affected. Moreover, emigrationR (i.e. accumulated outflow) is more strongly linked to a country’s research visibility than immigrationP (i.e. accumulated inflow). These findings have broad implications for resource allocation in migraNtion research, its societal relevance, and the need for more evidence-based policy debates on migrationI. I T R Introduction A Migration research has largely centered on subjects, locations, and priorities of interest to higher- income countries (Amelung et al., 2024; Schmiz et al., 2022, Collins, 2022; Pisarevskaya et al., 2020). However, the extent and underlying dynamics of this uneven research distribution remain poorly understood. The persistent underrepresentation of topics, populations, and regions in migration research not only marginalises scholars from other research actors (e.g., international and private sector) (Amelung et al., 2024), but also decreases the academic impact on policy making (Natter & Welfens, 2024), ultimately hindering global development efforts (SDG, 2024). Disparities in scientific production stem from differences in institutional capacity and research resources across countries (Akbaritabar, Castro Torres, et al., 2024; Castro Torres & Alburez-Gutierrez, 2022). The institutionalisation of migration studies has led to a geographically concentrated research infrastructure, with journals, authors, and publications disproportionately clustered in certain regions (Levy ARTICLE IN PRESS et al., 2020; Piccoli et al., 2023; Pisarevskaya et al., 2020). This uneven distribution is driven by global economic disparities that shape scientific production across fields (Castro Torres & Alburez-Gutierrez, 2022; Krause, 2016; Mayblin & Turner, 2020). Research output and influence largely depend on available resources, perpetuating global inequalities in knowledge production (Akbaritabar, Castro Torres, et al., 2024; Collyer, 2018; Gomez et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022). Research on higher-income countries receives more citations than comparable research elsewhere (Nielsen et al., 2018; Gomez et al., 2022). Wealthy countries are in an advantageous position: i) greater resources and staff producing research primarily focused on their own contexts; ii) produce more data that enables researchers from other regions to study their context; iii) higher scientific productivity, prestige, and connections, allowing them to set the research agenda and position themselves at the forefront of it. Due to uneven resources reflected in wealth and geographic disparities, scholars have pointed to S the disparities of the field (Natter & Welfens, 2024; Piccoli et Sal., 2023; Pisarevskaya et al., 2020). Migration research is intellectually organized around the priorEities of higher-income countries, leaving R significant gaps that remain unaddressed. P The literature has identified limitations in migration research, particularly its fragmentation across N academic disciplines and methodologies (Levy et al., 2020; Pisarevskaya et al., 2020). While specialization I can be beneficial, this fragmentation may also contribute to the absence of a unifying theoretical framework E (De Haas, 2021; Massey et al., 1993), inadequate measurement approaches (Willekens et al., 2016), and a L limited capacity for critical reflection on missed research opportunities (Amelina, 2021; Dahinden et al., C 2021). Because of this fragmentatiIon, the extent of the disparity remains unclear. It is uncertain whether T these imbalances are isolated or applicable across all scientific publications discussing migration-related R topics. A This paper examines the extent to which migration research disproportionately focuses on specific countries and regions, while neglecting others. In particular, it explores the underrepresentation of lower- income countries, accounting for both immigration and emigration levels. To do so, it provides a comprehensive view of global scientific production on migration and its change over time. Our study spans all scientific disciplines, identifying the countries being studied as well as the affiliations of contributing authors. Moreover, we compare our results with the actual global distribution of migrants, a key demographic factor that should shape research priorities. This allows us to identify over- and underrepresented countries. In addition, we explore how geographic location and economic factors influence the visibility of countries in migration research. The analysis leverages the Scopus bibliometric database of metadata on 36 million publications in the English language from 1996 to 2022 (Baas et al., 2020). Previous efforts to create a migration research corpus have relied on lists of migration journals, either by consulting experts in the field or by focusing on the highest impact factor journals (Levy et al., 2020; Pisarevskaya et al., 2020; Carling, 2015). While we consider expert knowledge and lists of migration journals, we extend this approach, which is often shaped by disciplinary bias, by developing a more comprehensive corpus that captures migration-related research beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries. This new corpus includes all scientific production engaging with migration, even if published in non-traditional outlets such as natural sciences or generalist journals. I T To ensure a comprehensive selection of migration-related articles and minimize potential biases R inherent in existing sources (such as the IMISCOE taxonomy, previous studies, and the MIGNEX and A MPIDR academic networks), we employed a parallel approach that combined text analysis techniques. First, we selected articles that contained terms from our glossary or word pairs in the title or abstract. Second, we relied on an anchor words approach (Akbaritabar & Rubin, 2024), which consisted of searching for new specific terms based on words that were used before and after our anchor word, i.e., the term ‘migra’. This helped to capture additional terms, or adjectives, related to migration, such as "chain migration" and "family migration" (as only a few examples) that might have been overlooked previously. We then reviewed the list of all terms obtained through this method and included them in our search list for migration-related terms. Additionally, we took a bottom-up, inductive approach, to extract all noun-phrase- clauses in the English language using the Spacy library (Montani et al., 2023), leveraging its pre-trained models based on large corpora of text in the English language, such as social media, Wikipedia, and similar sources. This approach enabled us to identify possible combinations of words that were not included in our list. Examples of such identified noun-phrase clauses include “mixed second-generation migrants”, “non- ARTICLE IN PRESS Western migrants”, “marriage migrants”, “marriage migration”, and “family migration” some of which were also captured using the anchor words approach described above, further confirming that our bottom- up approach complements well the deductive and top-down approach. Additionally, we scored all publications in corpus B using 18 criteria (see Table S.1), such as the total count of unique specific and general terms. We then selected those with scores within one standard deviation of the average score in publications from journals that mainly publish on migration topics (Figure S.1). These “migration journals” were defined as those containing the term “migr” in their name (e.g., International Migration Review) (smallest circle in Figure 1). We manually excluded irrelevant journals, such as those containing the term ‘migraine’ in the title. We use the distribution of scores from the relevant journals to guide the selection of the generalist and non-social science journals. Nonetheless, we also S evaluated publications with exceptionally high or low scores to ensure that scores from migration journals S do not distort the selection process, especially in cases where specific terms or concepts may be E disproportionately used. The indicator considers two components. The first component reflects the annual research salience of each country, defined as the number of unique mentions of a country across all publications each year. [ Please insert Figure 6 about here ] Discussion Scholars have suggested and presented anecdotal evidence of a disparity in terms of country research on migration (Amelung et al., 2024; Collyer, 2018; Schmiz et al., 2022). This disparity can be responsible for the generation of a series of biases e.g., West-Euro-centric bias, destination-country biases (Bakewell, 2008; Beauchemin, 2014; Erdal et al., 2023; Natter & Welfens, 2024; Schewel, 2020) that reflect persisting global inequalities in the infrastructure of scientific knowledge production (Akbaritabar, Castro Torres, et al., 2024; Collyer, 2018; Gomez et al., 2022b; Zhang et al., 2022). This article provides the first systematic ARTICLE IN PRESS empirical attempt to measure, identify, and explain the extent of this disparity of country research representation at a global level. We analysed persisting missed opportunities in migration research. We identified missed opportunities using a measure of country representation that combined yearly migration stocks and levels of research salience. We investigated whether migration research disproportionately studies specific geographic contexts while ignoring others with greater demographic relevance, e.g., in terms of the size of migrant population. We also provide an analysis of what factors contribute to this underrepresentation in migration research. Our results showed that lower income countries, and those with lower research investment as a share of GDP have the highest probability of being underrepresented. This result holds for measures of country research salience and when controlling for immigration and emigration levels. Higher income S countries are disproportionately overrepresented in migration reseaSrch. Countries with lower wealth and research allocation in GDP are less researched despite having larEger immigration and emigration stocks. R We showed a geographic concentration of research in specific continents (i.e. Americas, Europe, P and Asia), as well as important heterogeneities within them that persist over time. Although some countries N and subregions in Asia have been gaining more research salience, countries in North America and Europe I tend to concentrate the majority of salience. In line with previous research focusing on the role of research E infrastructure (e.g., financial investment, dedicated migration institutes) (Krause, 2016; Piccoli et al., 2023), L we confirm and provide quantitative estimates of the fundamental role of economic development and C research investment. I T We showed that country research salience is closely related to the authors’ country of affiliation. R Studying the composition of research salience by authors’ affiliation shows that high income countries are A not only the most researched and the ones concentrating the majority of authors, but also the ones that drive which countries are explored in other income groups. While on a superficial level this may not be problematic, case study selection within the lower-income countries could be influenced by high income countries interests. Countries with less politicised borders and populations that are still highly relevant from a demographic perspective may be persistently left behind in the global research agenda (Bakewell, 2008). Additionally, lower income countries may not always benefit from research conducted by high income ones. This could be mainly “helicopter research” where data and fieldwork come from the lower-income countries, but credit and reputation benefits go to the higher-income ones, a legacy of the colonial era on scientific collaboration (Basalla, 1967; Boshoff, 2009). However, many scholars in higher-income countries (who might study lower-income countries as a topic) come from lower-income countries themselves, something that could in principle explain some of the attention from higher-income countries to lower-income countries and requires further research. ARTICLE IN PRESS This study has certain limitations that we would like to acknowledge. While we set out to measure, identify, and explain the concentration of migration research salience in terms of underrepresented countries, there are various other gaps to be identified systematically, such as populations, topics, epistemologies and methods, among others (Castro Torres & Akbaritabar, 2024; Torres & Akbaritabar, 2025). Additionally, we used Scopus bibliometric data for our analysis that, while having one of the largest coverages among available databases and covering non-English publications, has an overrepresentation of English publications (Baas et al., 2020). Additionally, our searched keywords and phrases with multiple terms were in English. There are other bibliometric databases with more comprehensive coverage. For instance, the recent OpenAlex (Priem et al., 2022), which is in need of further quality control on missing metadata, such as abstracts and titles (Haupka et al., 2024). While Scopus is prone to limitations, it still offers possibilities that are not as developed in other databases, such as Clarivate’s Web of Science (WOS) S or OpenAlex. These include author name and affiliation disambiguaStion that we use for part of our analysis to connect the region of study in the migration-related literaturEe with the authors’ country of affiliation. R Additionally, previous research has shown that OpenAlex maximises the coverage but mostly in favor of P the largest science producers (Akbaritabar, Theile, et al., 2024; Castro Torres, 2024; Torres & Akbaritabar, N 2025). For instance, while in OpenAlex the coverage is higher, still, the largest countries in terms of I affiliation of authors and the number of publications produced match the largest countries in Scopus, WOS, E and similar. While this larger coverage has benefits in terms of content covered, as shown in the literature, L it still does not address the documented inequality and stratification among science-producing countries C and scholars, and it is shown in Ithe literature that OpenAlex’s larger coverage while improving the T conditions does not resolve the dominance of English publications and metadata over non-English data R which are still the minority in this database (Torres & Akbaritabar, 2025). Future research could extend our A analysis using such additional data sources to investigate whether the conditions for migration-related research are different. Finally, while we find that for the period 1996-2022, Ukraine is underrepresented (Figure 2), migration research on the country changed from 2022 onwards due to the refugee and migrant population generated by the conflict, something that we do not measure in this article. Implications of our study, and ways of addressing them, are diverse and challenging. Providing a global overview of how salience in migration research is distributed across countries and regions is one step to improve understanding of which countries are being overlooked by scholars. With this overview in place, next steps could study semantic and research agendas gaps in a global perspective. It is important to encourage researchers to reflect on the theories and generalizations that have emerged in this field, which are often concentrated along geographies that are not necessarily the most exposed by immigration and emigration dynamics. These results may seem counterintuitive when compared to societal expectations about what should be researched. Public imagination on migration often focuses on those coming from ARTICLE IN PRESS Africa or the Middle East, the type of regions that are underrepresented in migration research (Amelung et al., 2024; Collyer, 2018; Schmiz et al., 2022). Future studies could examine country pairs within publications to assess whether regions with higher salience (e.g., Europe) are associated with greater coverage of less salient regions (e.g., Africa). In this sense, the prominence of Western and higher-income contexts would not be entirely unexpected. Improving country representation in future research will help capture the diverse realities of migration and mobility processes. More concretely, our results may be used to support a more inclusive research agenda, in which countries that are important in terms of their migrant populations receive more attention. One fundamental task is to improve training, academic, and data infrastructures for migration research, as limited data associated with existing inequities in this area contribute to the underrepresentation of certain countries in the field (Meissner & and Taylor, 2024; Willekens et al., 2016). The task of identifying missed opportunities in migration research is a relevant but S also challenging one. By addressing them, researchers may contribuSte to decreasing persisting knowledge, policy and epistemological gaps (Natter & Welfens, 2024). Here,E funding agencies could play a crucial role R in setting the agenda and foster a more equal representation of different countries and contexts in migration P research. These agencies' emphasis on open access publishing would also enable a more equalized access N to research output and strengthen future migration research on underexplored contexts. JSON: Name: migration_research_equity_pipeline Title: A bibliometric and quantitative pipeline to measure and explain country-level inequities in migration research representation Short Hypothesis: Higher national research investment (research expenditure as percentage of GDP) causes greater country research salience in migration literature, controlling for population and migration stocks. Related Work: Existing approaches to mapping migration research rely primarily on either expert-curated journal lists or simple keyword searches. Expert-curated lists reduce false positives but are discipline- and journal-biased and miss migration-relevant publications in generalist and non-social-science outlets. Keyword-only retrievals increase coverage but suffer from noisy matches (e.g., animal or cellular 'migration'), limited handling of multiword concepts, and English-term bias. Recent work has introduced anchor-word expansion and NLP-based noun-phrase extraction to expand recall, and some studies combine bibliometrics with demographic indicators, but these typically focus on limited time windows, a subset of journals, or do not disambiguate country mentions versus author affiliations. Other work comparing bibliographic databases highlights coverage and metadata quality trade-offs across Scopus, Web of Science, and OpenAlex. Limitations remaining across methods include disciplinary skew, English-language dominance, lack of reproducible demonym-based country assignment, inadequate validation against human-labeled corpora, and limited modeling of economic and geographic determinants. Abstract: This pipeline operationalizes a reproducible method to quantify global inequities in migration research at the country level. The pipeline integrates: (1) an expansive retrieval step combining a top-down migration taxonomy with anchor-word expansion and bottom-up noun-phrase extraction to build a high-recall candidate corpus from bibliographic metadata; (2) a rule- and score-based filter calibrated on migration-specialist journals and a human-labeled validation sample to remove non-relevant uses of 'migration'; (3) demonym-based country mention extraction and disambiguation to assign countries of study; (4) author-affiliation disambiguation to measure researcher location; and (5) construction of annual research representation indicators linking research salience with migration stocks and population, followed by multivariable regression analyses to estimate economic and geographic determinants. The main contribution is an end-to-end, validated, and reproducible pipeline yielding both a cleaned corpus and quantitative indicators that identify under- and overrepresented countries, and estimate the effect of research investment and migration dynamics on research visibility. Expected outcomes include a ranked, explainable map of missed opportunities in migration research and associated determinants for policy and funding prioritization. Experiments: Datasets: Scopus metadata (titles, abstracts, journal, year, author affiliations) 1996-2022 (~36M records; initial candidate retrieval expected ~6.6M; final pipeline target ~120-130k migration publications); UN-DESA international migrant stock data 1996-2022; World Bank WDI: GDP per capita, R&D expenditure (% GDP), population (annual); optional comparative dataset: OpenAlex metadata for replication. Gold labels: random stratified sample of 2,000 candidate abstracts manually annotated for 'migration-related' and for country-of-study mentions. Baselines: (A) expert-journal-list retrieval; (B) keyword-only retrieval using root terms (e.g., 'migra*'); (C) noun-phrase-only retrieval; (D) OpenAlex corpus retrieval. Pipeline steps to evaluate: full pipeline (taxonomy+anchor expansion+noun-phrases+score filtering+demonym extraction); ablations removing one component at a time (no anchor expansion; no noun-phrase extraction; no scoring filter; no demonym assignment). Evaluation metrics: corpus retrieval: precision, recall, F1 against gold labels; coverage: total migration publications and unique country mentions; disambiguation error rates for demonyms and affiliations; representation classification: confusion matrix comparing Annual Research Representation quantiles vs manual country relevance labels (sample). Statistical modeling: dependent variable yearly country research salience (log count) and categorical under/overrepresentation indicator; models: OLS with clustered SE by country, negative binomial for counts, multinomial logit for representation categories. Model evaluation: R^2 / pseudo-R^2, RMSE, AIC/BIC, coefficient significance (p<0.05), variance inflation factors for multicollinearity. Comparative experiments: compare models including (i) emigration only, (ii) immigration only, (iii) both; and compare models with GDP vs research investment as predictors. Cross-validation: time-sliced validation (train on 1996-2016, test on 2017-2022) and 5-fold cross-validation on non-time models. Ablation study: measure change in retrieval F1 and in key model coefficients and predictive performance when removing each pipeline component. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Data bias: Scopus and English-language keyword lists overrepresent English-language and high-income-country publications; replication on other databases may yield different coverage. 2) Demonym ambiguity: country demonyms and ethnic terms may be ambiguous (shared names, homonyms), producing false positives/negatives in country assignment. 3) Non-human migration noise: some domain uses (animal, cellular) may persist despite filters. 4) Affiliation disambiguation errors: incorrect mapping of author institutional locations may bias measures of author composition. 5) Migration stock measurement error: UN stock estimates have uncertainty and inconsistent coverage across years and countries. 6) Observational inference limits: OLS and count models cannot establish causality; omitted confounders (e.g., language of publication, journal editorial policy, funding flows) can bias coefficient estimates. 7) Scalability and compute: processing millions of abstracts with NLP and noun-phrase extraction requires substantial compute and memory; resource limits may force sampling. 8) Temporal metadata gaps: missing abstracts or inconsistent author affiliation timestamps reduce effective sample size and temporal accuracy. 9) Generalizability: pipeline tuned on Scopus and English terms may not generalize to non-English literature or alternative bibliographic systems without re-tuning. 10) Human labeling limits: gold-label sample size and annotator disagreement constrain validation reliability.
